page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement), sentence beginning 'A minimal benchmark runs 40 rps'
quoted_clause: A minimal benchmark runs 40 rps — a saturation run on one host (6.5× the ~56,500 tok/s prefill ceiling at 100% MFU — theoretical peak), whose queue is expected to grow
observed: The 56,500 tok/s figure is the case-(i) (2N-only) ceiling, but it is introduced here without that qualifier, while §6 states that at the canonical 9,200-token context the ceiling is ≈48,000 tok/s (case (ii)) and ≈52,000 (case (iii)). A reader who takes 56,500 as 'the prefill ceiling' at the canonical context will mis-state the host's headroom by 18%. The 6.5× ratio itself is correct for case (i) (368,000/56,500 = 6.51), so only the label needs fixing.
root_cause: The case convention is introduced in §3 and not carried into §4, where the same ceiling is quoted without its convention.
correction: Write 'the ~56,500 tok/s case-(i) (2N-only) prefill ceiling at 100% MFU — theoretical peak; at the canonical context the attention-adjusted ceiling is ≈48,000 tok/s (§6)', or simply reference §6's number.
acceptance_test: Every occurrence of the prefill ceiling in the chapter carries its case convention, and the 6.5× ratio is stated with the same convention.

page_hint: Ch15 §3 (Worked Example), KV-cache-footprint paragraph, sentence beginning 'Doubling context to 19,000 tokens'
quoted_clause: Doubling context to 19,000 tokens pushes per-user KV to ~49.8 GB (19,000 × 2.62 MB) and halves on-host concurrency to ~8.7 (436 GB ÷ 49.8 GB; conservative integer floor 8).
observed: 436 ÷ 49.8 = 8.755, which rounds to 8.8, not 8.7; using the unrounded per-token value (19,000 × 2,621,440 B = 49.807 GB) gives 8.754, again 8.8. The neighbouring figure in the same paragraph, 436 ÷ 24.9037 = 17.507, is correctly rounded to 17.5. The two roundings in one paragraph are inconsistent (one rounds, one truncates). No downstream decision is affected — the conservative integer floor is 8 either way — so this is a presentation inconsistency rather than an error.
root_cause: Mixed rounding conventions within a single paragraph.
correction: Use '≈8.8' (or '≈8.75') to match the rounding used for 17.5, and keep the conservative integer floor of 8.
acceptance_test: Both concurrency figures in the paragraph are rounded by the same rule.

page_hint: Ch15 §3 (fleet screen) vs §4 (admission capacity)
quoted_clause: §3: '6.5 hosts at 100% MFU → 6.5 ÷ 0.35 = 18.6 → 19 hosts at the 35% MFU planning screen (case (i))' ... §4: 'report p95 only at offered loads ≤ the host's admission capacity, ~2 rps per host: 17 slots ÷ 8.6 s'
observed: The chapter derives two per-host capacity numbers that are close but not equal, and never reconciles them: the KV-slot route gives 17/8.6 = 1.98 rps/host, while the FLOP route gives 7.912e15 × 0.35 ÷ 1.4e11 ÷ 9,200 = 2.15 rps/host. Consequently 19 hosts cover 37.6 rps by the first route and 40.9 rps by the second — i.e. the 19-host screen is either marginally short of the 40 rps canonical peak or has 2% headroom, depending on which derivation is used. The chapter presents 19 hosts as a settled planning screen without noting that it sits within 6% of the peak under one reading.
root_cause: Two independent capacity derivations (KV-residency-limited and FLOP-limited) are used in adjacent sections without a stated binding constraint, so the reader cannot tell which one sets the host count.
correction: State which constraint binds at the canonical operating point and note the other as a co-limiter; if the KV-limited 1.98 rps/host binds, say so and note that 19 hosts covers 37.6 rps, i.e. the peak requires 21 hosts at that operating point (or that the peak is served with a small queueing margin).
acceptance_test: The chapter names the binding per-host constraint, and the stated host count is shown to cover the 40 rps peak under that constraint.

page_hint: Ch15 §5 (Common Mistakes), first bullet
quoted_clause: Over‑provisioning batch size to chase throughput: Increasing batch size improves TFLOPS utilization but degrades p99 latency because tail requests wait for larger chunks to fill.
observed: The stated mechanism — requests waiting for a batch to fill — describes static (fixed-batch) batching, not the continuous batching the chapter recommends in §6. Under continuous batching, a request joins the next scheduler iteration and never waits for a batch to fill; the latency cost of a larger batch comes from a longer per-step duration (higher ITL/TPOT for every in-flight request) and from increased queueing delay, not from fill-waiting. The chapter elsewhere (§4) gives the correct mechanism ('inter-request token interleaving ... scheduler fairness/queueing delay'), so §5 and §4 disagree on why the mistake happens.
evidence: §4: 'beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises ... because kernel launch overhead is amortized but inter-request token interleaving increases per-step HBM traffic and scheduler fairness/queueing delay'. §5: 'tail requests wait for larger chunks to fill'.
root_cause: The common-mistake bullet was written from the intuition of static batching and not reconciled with the continuous-batching model the chapter teaches.
correction: Rewrite the mechanism: 'because a larger decode batch lengthens the per-step duration, so every in-flight request sees a higher ITL/TPOT, and because queueing delay grows with the number of requests sharing the step.' If the fill-waiting mechanism is worth keeping, scope it explicitly to static batching.
acceptance_test: The mechanism named in §5 matches the mechanism named in §4 and is consistent with the continuous-batching model introduced in §6.

page_hint: Ch15 §5 (Common Mistakes), fourth bullet
quoted_clause: Neglecting kernel launch overhead: In dynamic‑batching setups, each new token generation can trigger a kernel launch. Without continuous batching or token‑level fusion, the kernel‑launch overhead (illustratively ~10–20 % of GPU time on H100-class parts at this traffic) can artificially depress measured MFU.
observed: Continuous batching does not reduce the number of kernel launches per decode step; it reduces idle gaps between batches and lets the scheduler keep the device busy. The mechanisms that actually remove per-step launch overhead are CUDA-graph capture and kernel fusion (which the chapter names elsewhere as 'token-level fusion'). As written, the sentence credits continuous batching with a benefit it does not provide, in a chapter whose §6 recommends continuous batching as the fix for a different symptom.
evidence: Per decode step, the launch count is set by the number of kernels in the model forward (tens to low hundreds), independent of how requests are batched; continuous batching changes when steps are issued, not how many kernels each step contains.
root_cause: Two distinct overheads — launch overhead and idle-gap overhead — are conflated under the label 'kernel launch overhead'.
correction: Separate them: 'each decode step issues a fixed set of kernels regardless of batch composition, so per-step launch overhead is a fixed cost that continuous batching does not remove; it is removed by CUDA-graph capture or kernel fusion. Continuous batching instead removes idle gaps between batches, which is a different saving.'
acceptance_test: The bullet names the mechanism that actually reduces launch overhead, and does not credit continuous batching with it.

page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement), sentence beginning 'beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises'
quoted_clause: beyond batch‑4 the p95 latency typically rises (implying a knee near batch 4) because kernel launch overhead is amortized but inter‑request token interleaving increases per‑step HBM traffic and scheduler fairness/queueing delay
observed: The stated cause is imprecise. Per-step HBM traffic does grow with batch (140 + 24.9B GB per step), but per-token traffic falls (140/B + 24.9 GB/token), so 'increases per-step HBM traffic' does not by itself explain a latency increase — it explains a throughput increase. The mechanism that raises latency is that a larger batch lengthens the step duration, so each in-flight request's inter-token latency grows (ITL = step time), with queueing delay as a secondary effect. The chapter's own bytes/token model (140/B + KV) makes this precise and should be used.
evidence: bytes/token = 140/B + 24.9 GB: B=1 → 164.9; B=4 → 59.9; B=16 → 33.65; B=32 → 29.28. Step time = (140 + 24.9B)/26,800 s: B=4 → 25.2 ms; B=16 → 42.0 ms; B=32 → 82.6 ms. ITL grows with B even though bytes/token falls.
root_cause: The chapter has a precise bytes/token model available but describes the batch-size latency effect in terms of traffic volume rather than step duration.
correction: Replace the traffic clause with the step-duration clause: 'because a larger batch lengthens the decode step (per-step traffic 140 + 24.9B GB), so every in-flight request's inter-token latency grows even though bytes/token falls (140/B + 24.9 GB/token); queueing delay and fairness effects add to this.'
acceptance_test: The stated mechanism is consistent with the chapter's own bytes/token and step-time arithmetic, and a reader can predict the direction of ITL change from the batch size.

page_hint: Ch15 §4 (Measurement), sentence beginning 'On the FlashAttention "traffic reduction" claim'
quoted_clause: one often sees (the figures below are hypothetical, not a cited measurement) a FlashAttention‑class kernel reported at a *different achieved HBM bandwidth* than a naive SDPA kernel (illustratively FlashAttention‑class ~400 GB/s achieved vs naive SDPA ~150 GB/s achieved for 9,200‑token contexts)
observed: The framing 'one often sees' presents the two numbers as typical reported values, but they are 12% and 4.5% of H100's 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth — far below what attention kernels typically achieve on that part, and low enough that a reader who treats them as 'typical' will badly underestimate the achievable rate and the size of the traffic reduction. The parenthetical 'hypothetical, not a cited measurement' contradicts the 'one often sees' framing in the same sentence. Either the framing or the numbers should change.
root_cause: The sentence was written to make a units point (rate vs bytes) and inherited placeholder numbers that are inconsistent with the framing sentence.
correction: Either drop 'one often sees' and keep the numbers explicitly as deliberately conservative placeholders ('for illustration, suppose a FlashAttention-class kernel sustains ~400 GB/s and a naive SDPA kernel ~150 GB/s — these are placeholders, not measurements, and are far below the H100's 3.35 TB/s peak'), or replace them with realistic achieved-bandwidth figures and cite them.
acceptance_test: The framing sentence and the numbers agree: either the numbers are presented as placeholders with no 'one often sees' claim, or they are realistic and sourced.

page_hint: Ch15, Fig 15.2 caption and the paragraph immediately following it ('The capacity response to batch size under peak load')
quoted_clause: They are not competing on the same axis: the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching.
observed: The statement is true of the bottleneck (decode remains bandwidth-bound) but incomplete in a way that matters for the figure's own right-hand panel. Prefix caching frees KV capacity (fewer recomputed prefixes, more room for active sequences), which raises the achievable concurrency and therefore the decode batch size, which raises decode goodput — the very quantity plotted on the right. The chapter's own §3 establishes KV capacity as the binding constraint on concurrency, so the two levers are coupled through KV capacity even though they act on different phases. The figure's framing ('two levers, two serving phases') would be more useful with the coupling stated.
evidence: §3: on-host concurrency is set by the 436 GB KV budget (17.5 requests at 9,500 tokens); §6: FP8 KV quantization doubles concurrency to 35.0. Any mechanism that frees KV capacity raises the batch size available to the decode path.
root_cause: The 'independent levers' framing was adopted to prevent the reader from treating prefix caching and batching as substitutes, and the coupling through KV capacity was not added back.
correction: Qualify the sentence: 'the decode bottleneck itself is unaffected by caching — but the two levers are coupled through KV capacity: prefix caching frees KV blocks, which can raise the achievable concurrency and therefore the decode batch size, so the right-hand curve can shift when the left-hand lever is pulled. The coupling is a capacity effect, not a compute effect.'
acceptance_test: The text states whether the two levers are independent, and if coupled, names the coupling resource and its direction.

page_hint: Ch15, 'The Optimization Decision Map', row 3 ('KV exhaustion / low concurrency')
quoted_clause: KV exhaustion / low concurrency | memory capacity | KV bytes/token, context distribution, fragmentation, active sequences | GQA/MQA (architecture-fixed — not a runtime lever; requires a re-checkpointed model), KV quantization, PagedAttention, context reduction, eviction/offload, prefix reuse
observed: PagedAttention is listed under a bottleneck labelled 'memory capacity', but it does not reduce the mathematical or allocated size of the KV state — it reduces fragmentation and allocator waste, so it raises usable capacity without lowering bytes/token. The chapter is explicit elsewhere that PagedAttention is a memory-management strategy rather than a size reduction, and §3's KV arithmetic is built on bytes/token. Listing it without that distinction risks the reader misconception that PagedAttention 'makes the KV cache smaller'.
evidence: §3's concurrency arithmetic is bytes/token × requests ≤ 436 GB; PagedAttention changes only the packing efficiency of that budget, so it moves the achievable request count without changing 2.62 MB/token.
root_cause: The row's bottleneck cell names only one of the two bottlenecks its own evidence column measures (fragmentation is listed as evidence but not as a bottleneck).
correction: Annotate the mechanism cell, e.g. 'PagedAttention (reduces fragmentation waste, not bytes/token)', and/or split the row's bottleneck cell into 'raw KV capacity' and 'fragmentation / allocator waste'.
acceptance_test: A reader cannot conclude from the map that PagedAttention reduces the per-token KV footprint; the map's bottleneck cell names every bottleneck its evidence column measures.

page_hint: Ch15 §6 (Architecture Consequence), decision (3), vs §5 (Common Mistakes), second bullet
quoted_clause: §6: '(3) KV cache management via FP8 KV quantization (≈2.62 → ~1.31 MB/token — exactly 50% of FP16 by raw tensor byte-halving, cutting a 9,500-token per-user KV to ~12.45 GB ...)' ... §5: '**KV quantization** is a separate, orthogonal lever that cuts the per-token footprint without changing context length or the attention window; it introduces a numerical approximation (FP8 rounding) that must be quality-validated (Ch 14) before it is relied on'
observed: §5 makes quality validation a precondition for relying on FP8 KV quantization; §6 adopts it as an architecture decision and derives a concurrency figure (17.5 → 35.0) from it without carrying the precondition. The decision map's weight-quantization row carries an explicit 're-run the SLO and quality test after the change' instruction, but the KV-quantization row does not, so the map and §6 are both weaker than §5 on this point.
evidence: §5: 'must be quality-validated (Ch 14) before it is relied on (FP8 ≈2.62 → ~1.31 MB/token ...)'. §6: the same FP8 KV figure is used to compute 436/12.45 = 35.0 concurrent requests with no validation gate.
root_cause: The decision section was written from the capacity arithmetic and did not carry the quality gate that the mistakes section established.
correction: Add the gate to §6 decision (3) and to the map's KV-quantization cell, e.g. 'FP8 KV quantization — adopt only after the quality test (Ch 14) passes; the concurrency figure below assumes the quality gate is met.'
acceptance_test: Every place FP8 KV quantization is relied upon for a capacity or latency figure carries the quality-validation precondition stated in §5.

page_hint: Ch15 §6 (Architecture Consequence), sentence beginning 'the single-host upper end is capped by'
quoted_clause: the single-host upper end is capped by the 100%-MFU parameter-matmul-only ceiling: 7.91×10¹⁵ FLOP/s ÷ 1.4×10¹¹ FLOP/token ≈ 56,500 tok/s under the linear-only case (i) — a 2N-only figure; at the canonical 9,200-token context the attention term (§3, case ii) lowers this to ≈48,000 tok/s
observed: The sentence names 56,500 tok/s as the cap and then immediately lowers the cap to 48,000, so 'capped by' and the number that follows do not agree. The arithmetic is right; the sentence structure is not. A reader scanning for the host's ceiling can easily take 56,500 as the answer.
root_cause: The sentence was extended (case i → case ii → case iii) without restructuring the lead clause.
correction: Restructure: 'the single-host ceiling is set by the 100%-MFU FLOP bound: ≈56,500 tok/s under the linear-only case (i), reduced to ≈48,000 tok/s at the canonical 9,200-token context once the attention term is included (case ii), and ≈52,000 tok/s under the causal case (iii).'
acceptance_test: The sentence's lead clause names the same number that the sentence's conclusion establishes as the cap.

page_hint: Ch 16 §3 (Worked Example → Mode 2 — cloud GPU instances), paragraph beginning 'The cloud case is a family, not a single line.'
quoted_clause: For example, a mid-case with ~6 reserved warm hosts + ~15 burst hosts held for ~4 peak hours/day, at $20/hr (burst) and the warm pool at a reserved rate, lands between the two endpoints
observed: The mid-case as specified does not land between the two named endpoints ($87.6K and $306.6K). It exceeds the upper endpoint, and its burst term is longer than the billing month it is priced against, so the configuration is not physically realizable as written.
evidence: Burst term: 15 hosts × 4 h/day × 260 workdays = 15,600 host-hours. The billing month contains only 730 h, and 4 h/day × 260 days = 1,040 h of burst per month > 730 h — the burst term alone is infeasible. Total: 4,380 (warm) + 15,600 (burst) = 19,980 host-hours × $20/hr = $399,600/mo = 1.30× the always-on-at-peak endpoint (21 × 730 × $20 = $306,600). Even if the warm pool were free, the burst term ($312,000) still exceeds the always-on endpoint. A month-consistent version (4 peak h/day × 21.67 business days = 86.7 h/mo) gives 15 × 86.7 = 1,300 burst h → 5,680 h → $113,600/mo ≈ $18.21/1K, which does fall between the endpoints. The chapter's own monthly-workday divisor (260 ÷ 12 = 21.67) is used correctly elsewhere in the same chapter.
root_cause: The mid-case was constructed by multiplying a per-day burst duration by the annual workday count (260) instead of the monthly workday count (21.67), and the resulting total was never checked against the two endpoints it is asserted to fall between.
correction: Restate the mid-case on a monthly basis: 4 peak h/day × 21.67 business days ≈ 86.7 h/mo; burst = 15 × 86.7 ≈ 1,300 host-hours; total ≈ 5,680 host-hours → ≈ $113.6K/mo ≈ $18.21/1K. State explicitly that the burst term is bounded by the 730-h month, and add one sentence asserting that the mid-case lies between $87.6K and $306.6K.
acceptance_test: Recompute 6×730 + 15×(4×21.67) = 5,680 host-hours; × $20 = $113,600; assert 87,600 < 113,600 < 306,600 and assert burst hours ≤ 730. The printed mid-case must satisfy both assertions.

page_hint: Ch 16 §8 mini-case — paragraphs 'The rate comparison hides the memory geometry…', 'The honest number:…', and the closing paragraph beginning 'Request volume is not the lever:'
quoted_clause: The two hosts clear the rate comparison, not the full-context KV budget. ... The honest number: self-hosting two servers ~$40K/month all-in vs ~$104K/month API at current volume (5M × $0.0208) — a **~$64K/month saving in favor of self-hosting** ... the two hosts are sized for a ~4 rps peak — 2 × the canonical ~1.9 rps per host
observed: The mini-case proves that the two-server configuration cannot hold the KV state for the stated workload, then prices it as a viable alternative, reports a $64K/mo saving in favor of self-hosting, and finally asserts a ~4 rps peak capacity for it. The capability failure and the cost conclusion are never reconciled; the closing decision rule ('self-host if the consumed engineer's time is worth less than ~$90K/month') therefore recommends buying a configuration the same mini-case has shown to be infeasible.
evidence: Mini-case's own numbers: 4 replicas × 140 GB = 560 GB of the 640 GB pool; after the ~64 GB runtime reserve, ~16 GB of KV remains = 0.64 of one 9,500-token request (24.9 GB). At 2 rps × 8.6 s ≈ 17 requests in flight, the KV requirement is 17 × 24.9 = 423 GB — 26× the 16 GB available; the configuration can hold zero full-context requests. The '~4 rps peak' claim is contradicted by the same arithmetic: 4 rps × 8.6 s = 34.4 in flight × 24.9 GB = 857 GB of KV required versus 16 GB available. The '640 GB pool' framing also misstates where KV lives: with 2 GPUs per replica each replica has 160 GB HBM − 140 GB weights = 20 GB for KV + runtime, so KV cannot be pooled across the host's four replicas.
root_cause: Two independent analyses (memory geometry and TCO) run in the same mini-case without a capability gate; the cost model silently assumes away the first analysis's conclusion, and the capacity claim is imported from the canonical TP=8 fleet rather than derived for the mini-case's TP=2 replica layout.
correction: Add an explicit capability gate before the TCO comparison and make the cost conclusion conditional on it. Recommended wording: 'The two-server configuration fails the KV screen for 9,500-token requests (16 GB of KV against 423 GB required at 17 in flight), so the $64K/mo figure compares an infeasible option with a feasible one and is not a realizable saving; the API is the only mode that can serve this workload as specified.' Restate the geometry per replica (2 GPUs = 160 GB, 140 GB weights, 20 GB for KV + runtime) rather than as a pooled 640 GB host pool. Delete or re-derive the '~4 rps peak' claim and the 'more volume widens the gap' argument that depends on it.
acceptance_test: The mini-case must contain an explicit statement of whether the two-server configuration can hold the in-flight KV for the stated request length, and the $64K/mo saving and the 'more volume widens the gap' claim must each be qualified by that statement. A reader must not be able to conclude that buying the two servers saves $64K/mo at the stated workload.

page_hint: Ch 15 §8 mini-case — sentence introducing the queueing-delay and token-throughput results
quoted_clause: drops from 320 ms (single host, batch‑1) to 140 ms (dual host, continuous batch) — both measured under saturation at the stated 12.5/50 rps offered load, and token throughput rises from ~8.5K to 70,000 tokens/s
observed: The 'measured under saturation' claim is inconsistent with the mini-case's own token arithmetic, and a bounded p95 queueing delay is not a saturation measurement. The sentence also conflates a capacity rate with an achieved throughput at the stated load.
evidence: At the 12.5 rps average with the canonical 9,500-token request, the offered token rate is 12.5 × 9,500 = 118,750 tok/s, which exceeds the two-host aggregate of 70,000 tok/s; the dual-host system can complete only 70,000/9,500 ≈ 7.4 rps of full-context requests, so it is under-served, not saturated, at 12.5 rps. Under the benign reading (the 50 rps peak arm), saturation is arithmetically plausible, but an overloaded queue grows without bound, so a stable p95 queueing delay of 320 ms cannot be a saturation measurement either. In both arms the 8.5K and 70,000 tok/s figures are capacity rates (the mini-case itself calls 8.5K 'the same prefill-dominated raw single-host rate'), not achieved throughput at the stated offered load.
root_cause: The mini-case reports a capacity benchmark (tokens/s at saturation) and an offered-load condition (12.5/50 rps) in the same sentence without distinguishing them, and then attaches the word 'saturation' to a queueing-delay statistic that is only meaningful below saturation.
correction: Separate the two claims: state the offered load the benchmark was driven at, state that the 8.5K and 70,000 tok/s figures are saturated capacity rates (tokens/s the host(s) can sustain), and state the queueing-delay measurement as taken at a load below saturation (or replace it with a saturation-queueing statement such as 'the queue grows without bound at 12.5 rps on one host'). If the benchmark was run at the 50 rps peak, say so and give the admitted completion rate (≈7.4 rps) alongside the token rate.
acceptance_test: Every throughput figure in the mini-case must be labelled either as a saturated capacity rate or as an achieved rate at a stated offered load, and the queueing-delay figure must be attached to a load at which the queue is stable. A reader must be able to tell which of the two the 8.5K and 70,000 tok/s numbers are.

page_hint: Ch 15, Table 15-1 — column header 'KV Cache / User (GB)' and the note beneath the table
quoted_clause: | KV Cache / User (GB) | ... | ~24.9 | ... KV‑Cache/User uses the canonical ~2.62 MB/token × 9,500 ≈ 24.9 GB.
observed: The column is labelled per user but its values are per request (one 9,500-token request's KV footprint). The chapter's own note repeats the mislabel. This contradicts the book's explicit distinction between users and in-flight requests.
evidence: 24.9 GB = 2.62 MB/token × 9,500 tokens = the KV of a single request. The 'KV demand ÷ host KV budget' column multiplies this value by in-flight requests (17 / 86 / 344), confirming the per-request basis. The table's own note states: 'never equate in-flight concurrency with a number of registered or simultaneously-online users' — so a per-user reading is excluded by the book's own definition. At the canonical 5% concurrency, a user's KV is 0.05 × 24.9 ≈ 1.25 GB, not 24.9 GB.
root_cause: The column header was written from the workload's user-centric framing rather than from the quantity actually tabulated (per-request KV footprint), and the note inherited the error.
correction: Rename the column 'KV per request (GB)' (or 'KV / in-flight request (GB)') and correct the note to 'KV per request uses the canonical ~2.62 MB/token × 9,500 ≈ 24.9 GB; the KV-demand column multiplies this by the in-flight request count.' If a per-user figure is wanted, add it as a separate, clearly labelled column (≈1.25 GB at 5% concurrency).
acceptance_test: No cell in Table 15-1 may be labelled 'per user' unless it is computed from the concurrency profile; the note beneath the table must use the same unit as the column header.

page_hint: Ch 15, Table 15-1 — column header 'prefill demand ÷ 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s)' and the adjacent 'Tokens' column
quoted_clause: | Tokens | ... | 9,500 | ... | prefill demand ÷ 100%-MFU para­meter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s) | ... | 0.33× | 1.63× | 6.51× |
observed: The prefill-demand ratios are computed on 9,200 input tokens per request, but the adjacent 'Tokens' column states 9,500 and the note says 'Tokens is tokens per request — the 9,500-token canonical context length'. A reader recomputing from the table's own numbers gets different values, and the discrepancy is material in the peak row.
evidence: Recomputation with 9,200 input tokens: 2 × 9,200/56,500 = 0.326 → 0.33×; 10 × 9,200/56,500 = 1.628 → 1.63×; 40 × 9,200/56,500 = 6.513 → 6.51× — all three printed values reproduce exactly. Recomputation with the table's stated 9,500 tokens: 0.336 → 0.34×; 1.681 → 1.68×; 6.726 → 6.73×. The typical row differs by 3.1% and the peak row by 3.4%, and the peak row's binding-constraint cell quotes '~6.5× demand over host peak'. The 56,500 tok/s ceiling itself is confirmed as the case-(i) linear-only ceiling (8 × 989 TFLOPS ÷ 140e9 FLOP/token = 56,514 tok/s), consistent with Ch 16's 19,780 tok/s/host at 35% MFU.
root_cause: The column header states the denominator but not the numerator's token basis, and the table's 'Tokens' column mixes total context (9,500) with the prefill-relevant input count (9,200) without distinguishing them.
correction: State the numerator basis in the column header, e.g. 'prefill demand (9,200 input tokens/req) ÷ 100%-MFU parameter-matmul ceiling (56,500 tok/s)', and rename the 'Tokens' column to 'Context tokens/req (9,500 = 9,200 in + 300 out)' so the two token counts are visibly different quantities.
acceptance_test: Every value in the prefill-demand column must be reproducible from the table's own printed numbers plus the stated numerator basis; recomputing with 9,500 tokens must not be the path a reader is led down.

page_hint: Fig 16.1 caption (end of Ch 16), 'Caveat:' sentence
quoted_clause: **Caveat:** break-even is a price sensitivity across $15–25 per 1,000 requests (≈$0.015–0.025 per request) — per-price crossovers (~6.2–10.4M), not an interval — not apples-to-apples
observed: The caption contradicts the body text on the nature of the break-even. The body insists repeatedly that the break-even is a region/range, not a point; the caption says the opposite.
evidence: Body, §16.3: 'the break-even is a **region**, not a point: the figure marks the [ILLUSTRATIVE] price band, and the honest output is a range (here ~6.2–10.4M req/mo) rather than a single "the break-even is 7.5M" claim.' Body, Note 16.1-1: 'The self-host line crosses the managed line over a **range** of ~6.2–10.4 M requests/mo'. Caption: 'per-price crossovers (~6.2–10.4M), **not an interval**'. The caption's own Takeaway also states a point ('crosses the managed API at ~7.5M req/mo'), which the body forbids as a standalone claim.
root_cause: The caption was written to compress the note and over-compressed: the intended point (the band is a set of per-price crossover points, not a statistical confidence interval) was expressed as a denial of the body's own framing.
correction: Rewrite the caveat to agree with the body: 'break-even is a price sensitivity across $15–25 per 1,000 requests (≈$0.015–0.025 per request): the per-price crossovers span ~6.2–10.4M req/mo, so the break-even is a region rather than a single volume; the ~7.5M point is the canonical-price crossover only.'
acceptance_test: The caption and the body must both describe 6.2–10.4M as a range/region of crossover volumes; no sentence in the chapter may describe the same quantity as 'not an interval'.

page_hint: Ch 16 §3, 'Parametric multi-region worksheet' table, row 3
quoted_clause: | 3 | Warmed capacity per region | N_region = ⌈λ_region·W_KV/(C·u·ρ)⌉ + N_spare (Table 17-1 formula, applied per region; each region is sized for λ_peak = 40 rps — the failover load — not its share λ_region; λ_region sets only the traffic split, which is what produces the ≥2× capacity term) | NOT SIZED (depends on rows 1–2) |
observed: The formula and its own parenthetical rule contradict each other: the formula sizes each region on λ_region, while the rule states each region is sized on λ_peak = 40 rps. A reader applying the printed formula gets a smaller per-region fleet than the rule requires, and the ≥2× capacity term does not follow from the formula as printed.
evidence: Applying the formula as printed with λ_region = α·40 gives N_region = ⌈α·40·8.6/(17·0.665)⌉ + N_spare, which for α < 1 is below the 31 working + 1 reserve hosts the failover rule requires. Applying the stated rule (λ_peak = 40 rps per region) gives ⌈344/11.305⌉ + 1 = 32 per region, so two regions = 64 hosts = 2× the 32-host single-region policy fleet — which is exactly the '≥2×' claim the row makes. The formula as printed cannot produce that number.
root_cause: The row was written by copying the Table 17-1 formula verbatim and then adding a sizing rule that the copied formula does not implement; the two were never reconciled.
correction: Write the formula to match the rule: N_region = ⌈λ_peak·W_KV/(C·u·ρ)⌉ + N_spare (each region sized for the full failover load λ_peak = 40 rps), and add a separate line or note showing the resulting ≥2× term (2 regions × 32 hosts = 64 vs 32 single-region). If λ_region is retained for the traffic split, label it as a traffic-share input only and show it nowhere in the sizing formula.
acceptance_test: Substituting the row's own rule into the row's own formula must reproduce the ≥2× capacity term quoted in the same row and in the multi-region paragraph above the table.

page_hint: Ch 16 §3, paragraph immediately after Table 16-1 ('None of A/A′/B/B′/C is scored as validated comparable')
quoted_clause: The three statuses are: `validated comparable` (measured on matched availability/failover/warm-capacity/SLO-goodput), `planning-only incomparable` (this table), and `fails requirement` (a mode that cannot meet the 99.9% multi-region SLA).
observed: The status vocabulary is internally inconsistent with the table it governs. By the book's own definition every row in Table 16-1 fails the requirement (all are single-region, none is priced for the 99.9% multi-region SLA), yet all are labelled 'planning-only incomparable'. Meanwhile the one row that demonstrably fails a requirement — row B, 6 hosts ≈ 11.9 rps against a 40 rps peak — has no status that fits it.
evidence: Table 16-1 rows A, A′, B, B′, C all carry the status 'planning-only, incomparable' and the table's own qualification for B states 'cannot serve the canonical peak'. The multi-region paragraph states that 'every $/1K figure in this chapter … prices a single-region deployment' and that the canonical SLA is 'UNSIZED and NOT PRICED'. So 'fails requirement' as defined is true of every row, and the third status is simultaneously unused and universally applicable.
root_cause: The status vocabulary was defined against the availability requirement only, while the table's rows are scored against several requirements (load-serving, availability, SLO-goodput); the definition was not re-checked against the rows it classifies.
correction: Redefine the third status against the requirement the table actually tests, e.g. 'fails load-serving requirement (a mode that cannot serve the canonical offered load under its stated provisioning)', and apply it to row B (6 hosts ≈ 11.9 rps < 40 rps peak). Add a sentence stating that no row is scored against the multi-region availability requirement at all, so 'fails requirement' in the availability sense is not evaluated in this table.
acceptance_test: Every row in Table 16-1 must map to exactly one status under the stated definitions, and the third status must be used at least once or explicitly declared out of scope for the table.

page_hint: Ch 16 §8 mini-case — sensitivity sentence beginning 'Sensitivity: at $156K/yr fully loaded…'
quoted_clause: Sensitivity: at $156K/yr fully loaded (0.5 FTE engineer → $6.5K/mo) self-host = 13.8 + 6.5 = $20.3K/mo — the verdict is robust to the rate; the $84K saving and the threshold margin are not.
observed: The claim that the threshold is not robust to the staff rate is false. The opportunity-cost threshold is algebraically invariant to the wage rate; only the cash saving changes. The book also misses the useful insight that the threshold is wage-independent.
evidence: Threshold derivation as printed: V* = API + wage − self-host = 104 + W − (13.9 + W) = 90.1K, independent of W. At W = 26K: 104 + 26 − 40 = 90.2K. At W = 6.5K: 104 + 6.5 − 20.4 = 90.1K. The cash saving does change (104 − 40 = 64K vs 104 − 20.4 = 83.6K ≈ 84K), so only the first half of the sentence is correct. The same invariance is visible in the Mode-1 staffing variant the mini-case already prints: 'On Mode 1's ~$10K/mo staff alloc the self-host cost is ~$23.8K/mo and the gap ~$80.2K/mo' — the implied threshold there is 104 + 10 − 23.9 = 90.1K, identical.
root_cause: The sensitivity was run on the cash-saving line only; the threshold was not re-derived under the alternative rate, and the sentence generalized from one quantity to two.
correction: Rewrite as: 'the verdict is robust to the rate: the cash saving moves from ~$64K to ~$84K, but the opportunity-cost threshold is unchanged at ~$90K/mo, because the wage appears on both sides of the comparison (104 + W − (13.9 + W)).' Add the invariance as an explicit teaching point — it tells the reader that the staffing rate changes the size of the prize, not the decision rule.
acceptance_test: Recompute the threshold at both wage rates ($26K/mo and $6.5K/mo) and confirm the printed threshold is identical; the text must not claim the threshold moves with the wage rate.
